description: Our team has built a new shift-and-stack system through interactive sonification, which even blind people can use! We intend to use this with blinking and ML for the ultimate asteroid detector, combining AI with real human work.
summary:
SONAR (SPHEREx Observations Narrated through Audio Rendering) is a web tool for finding moving asteroids in real SPHEREx images. Users blink through frames of one patch of sky and click the moving object in each. Then comes the original part: we turn shift-and-stack into sound. The frames are lined up along the object’s path, and how strongly the signal builds up becomes pitch and loudness, so a real asteroid can be heard. To our knowledge, using sonified shift-and-stack to verify asteroids is a new approach. An optional machine check then gives a second opinion, after the user has decided.

SPHEREx maps the whole sky repeatedly, so asteroids hide in its data as small changes over time. Blinking alone is hard: faint movers are easy to miss, mistakes are common, and blind or low-vision people are shut out. Hearing adds a second sense, so more people can check real NASA data.

Try it and join our testing: https://asteroid-research-study.vercel.app/#/
details:
What does it do, or how does it work?
SONAR loads real SPHEREx spectral images of one patch of sky taken hours apart. You blink between them and click the moving object in each frame. The tool then lines the frames up along that track (shift-and-stack) and plays a sound whose pitch and loudness rise when the signal adds up strongly. A rule-based check, and optionally a trained model, gives a second opinion only after you commit your verdict.

What benefits does it have?
It gives people a second sense for a task that is hard by eye alone. It supports blind and low-vision users, helps confirm faint movers, and uses real NASA data. The code is open source.

What is the intended impact?
To let students, citizen scientists and blind or low-vision people help check moving objects in SPHEREx data, and to give us a way to test whether looking, listening, or both works best.

What tools, languages or software did you use?
Python (NumPy, SciPy, Astropy) to process the SPHEREx FITS images, and JavaScript, HTML/CSS and the Web Audio API for the page. We used SPHEREx data from NASA-IPAC IRSA and JPL Horizons to check known asteroids such as 7 Iris. Claude (Anthropic) assisted with the code, and we note this in the repo.

How is your project creative?
Our main original idea is sonified shift-and-stack: instead of only looking at stacked images, people hear how strongly a track’s signal builds up, so faint asteroids that are hard to see can still be heard. It also makes the task usable by blind and low-vision people. Sound is used as a verification step, not decoration, and the human always decides before the machine gives its opinion.

What factors did your team consider?
SPHEREx frames change brightness by about 2x between exposures because each samples a different wavelength, so we re-measured our thresholds on SPHEREx data instead of reusing ground-based numbers. Within one 2-minute sequence, an asteroid barely moves, so we used frames hours apart. Results so far come from a small number of known asteroids, so we treat them as promising, not proven. We cite all sources, list our earlier asteroid-hunter work as prior work, and note that NASA does not endorse the project.
